title: Volume in the Real World
subtitle: Packing, filling and the question of what actually fits.
objectives: Apply the volume formula to practical problems
Combine volumes of more than one prism
Convert a calculated volume into litres

cards.title: Will it fit is a volume question, and a shape question
cards.text: Volume tells you whether there is enough room. It does not tell you whether the shape goes in. Both matter.

cards.title: Divide by a thousand
cards.text: Once you have cm³, litres are one short step away.
points: **cm³ ÷ 1,000 = litres.**
**A 30 × 20 × 10 cm box** is 6,000 cm³ = 6 litres.
**m³ × 1,000 = litres.**
**One bridge each way.**

question.text: A tank is 50 cm by 20 cm by 30 cm. How many litres? Digits only.

cards.title: Cut it into boxes
cards.text: An L-shape is not a formula. It is two prisms added together.
points: **Split it** into rectangular pieces.
**Work out each volume.**
**Add them.**
**Or find the big box and subtract** the missing piece.

cards.title: How much water is that?
cards.alt: A rectangular glass aquarium being filled with water, about a third full
cards.text: Length times width times height. Then decide whether to say it in litres.

cards.title: Your lungs hold about six litres
cards.text: Not all of it moves. A normal breath is far smaller than the total capacity.
points: **Total capacity** is roughly six litres in an adult.
**A quiet breath** moves about half a litre.
**Training raises how much you can move**, not the size of the chest.
**Six litres** is six of those 10 cm cubes.

cards.title: The cube, one more time
cards.text: Before the exam week, a last look at how fast volume climbs when an edge grows.

question.text: An L-shaped block is best handled by…
question.explain: Split, calculate each part, add. Or subtract the missing block from the full box.

cards.title: Boot space is quoted in litres for a reason
cards.text: A boot is not a neat box, so manufacturers measure it by filling it.
points: **They pack it with standard blocks** and count the volume.
**480 litres** is a typical family car.
**Shape still decides** whether your actual suitcase goes in.
**Volume is necessary, not sufficient.**

cards.title: Enough room is not the same as it goes in
cards.text: A 1 m pole has almost no volume and still will not fit in a shoebox.
points: **Check the volume first** — if it fails, stop.
**Then check each dimension** against the opening.
**Long thin things** fail on length, not volume.
**Two tests, in that order.**

question.text: A 20 × 20 × 20 cm box. How many litres? Digits only.

cards.title: Why a bigger fan box is mostly air
cards.text: Take a fan out of its packaging and it never goes back in easily.
points: **The box is sized for the assembled shape**, not the volume of parts.
**The guard is a sphere of mostly empty space.**
**Volume of material is tiny** compared with volume of box.
**Shipping pays for the air.**

terms.def: A shape made of more than one prism joined together.
Both having enough volume and having each dimension small enough.

cards.title: What to remember
points: cm³ ÷ 1,000 gives litres.
Composite shapes split into prisms, then add or subtract.
Enough volume does not mean it fits.
Check volume first, then each dimension.

quiz.text: A tank is 40 cm by 25 cm by 20 cm. How many litres? Digits only.
quiz.objective: Volume of cubes and rectangular prisms

quiz.text: How do you convert cm³ to litres?
quiz.explain: A litre is 1,000 cm³, so divide.
quiz.objective: Volume of cubes and rectangular prisms

quiz.text: An L-shaped solid is best found by…
quiz.explain: Split, calculate, add. Or subtract the missing block from a full box.
quiz.objective: Volume of cubes and rectangular prisms

quiz.text: A box is 10 cm by 10 cm by 10 cm. How many litres? Digits only.
quiz.objective: Volume of cubes and rectangular prisms

quiz.text: If an object's volume is less than a box's volume, it will always fit inside.
quiz.explain: A long thin pole has small volume and still will not go in. Dimensions matter too.
quiz.objective: Volume of cubes and rectangular prisms

quiz.text: A car boot of 480 litres is…
quiz.explain: Multiply by 1,000 to go from litres to cm³.
quiz.objective: Volume of cubes and rectangular prisms

quiz.text: Two stacked boxes, each 20 × 10 × 5 cm. Total volume in cm³? Digits only.
quiz.explain: Each is 1,000 cm³, so together 2,000 cm³.
quiz.objective: Volume of cubes and rectangular prisms

quiz.text: First check when asking whether something fits?
quiz.explain: If the volume fails, nothing else matters. Then check each dimension.
quiz.objective: Volume of cubes and rectangular prisms

quiz.text: A fish tank is 60 × 30 × 40 cm. How many litres? Digits only.
quiz.objective: Volume of cubes and rectangular prisms

quiz.text: A full box is 100 cm³ and a 20 cm³ piece is cut out. What remains?
quiz.explain: Subtract the missing piece from the whole.
quiz.objective: Volume of cubes and rectangular prisms

quiz.text: Why is a fan's box mostly empty space?
options: It is sized for the assembled shape, not the material
quiz.explain: The guard encloses a lot of air, and the box has to fit the whole shape.
quiz.objective: Volume of cubes and rectangular prisms

quiz.text: A 2 m by 1 m by 0.5 m container. Volume in m³? Use a decimal if needed.
quiz.objective: Volume of cubes and rectangular prisms

teacher.summary: Term 2 Week 10 Math, the last teaching week, taking the prism formula into use. Two ideas carry it: the cm³-to-litre bridge, which connects this fortnight to the conversion weeks, and composite shapes, which are taught as splitting rather than as a new formula. The fit card is the one worth keeping — enough volume is necessary and not sufficient, and the pole-in-a-shoebox case makes that obvious in a sentence. The fan packaging card closes the subject on something he has in the house.
discussion: How do you get from cm³ to litres?
Why can something fit on volume and still not go in?
How would you find the volume of an L-shaped block?
extension: Work out the volume of your room in m³ and in litres.
Measure a container, predict its litres, then fill it and check.
misconceptions: That volume alone decides whether something fits.
Multiplying instead of dividing for litres.
Looking for a formula for composite shapes.
